title: U.S. Economy Before vs. After Iran War: Five Revealing Charts Explain the Impact
body:
The United States entered the first day of its joint strike against Iran with an economy that, until the night before, appeared to be on a steady path toward lower inflation, cheaper energy and stronger consumer purchasing power. Data released on February 27 showed a modest decline in headline price growth, a modest easing of mortgage rates and a rebound in gasoline prices that had been hovering near historic lows. Those indicators, which had been the focus of analysts’ forecasts for the coming months, now sit against a backdrop of heightened geopolitical risk that could quickly reverse the modest gains the economy has enjoyed over the past year.

Inflation, which has been the dominant narrative in U.S. macro‑policy since mid‑2021, was finally showing signs of a sustained slowdown. The Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 0.2 percent in January, well below the 0.4‑percent increase that economists had expected. Core inflation – which strips out volatile food and energy costs – was down to 4.9 percent year‑over‑year, the lowest level since the early stages of the pandemic. The Federal Reserve, which has kept the policy rate at a 22‑year high of 5.25‑5.50 percent, signaled that a pause in further hikes was plausible, giving markets a brief reprieve after a year of aggressive tightening.

Energy markets, a critical driver of the inflation picture, were also trending in the right direction. Crude oil futures settled around $78 a barrel, a modest dip from the $85‑plus levels seen in late 2023. The corresponding drop in gasoline prices – averaging $3.12 per gallon nationally – translated into a tangible boost for households, especially those in the Midwest and South where commuting costs constitute a larger share of budgets. The lower fuel price helped curb the transportation component of the CPI, which had previously been a major source of upward pressure.

Consumer confidence, measured by the University of Michigan’s index, rose to 71.2 in February, its highest reading since 2022. The uptick reflected not only the easing of price pressures but also a robust labor market that continued to add roughly 200,000 jobs per month through the first quarter. Unemployment remained at a 50‑year low of 3.5 percent, and wage growth, though modest, stayed above inflation, giving workers real‑term buying power. Retail sales data for January showed a 0.4 percent increase, indicating that shoppers were still willing to spend despite lingering concerns about the future.

The sudden shift to a military confrontation, however, introduces a suite of variables that could quickly derail the positive trajectory. Historically, geopolitical crises have spurred spikes in oil prices as markets react to the risk of supply disruptions. A sustained escalation with Iran could tighten global oil supplies, pushing Brent crude back above $90 a barrel and reigniting inflationary pressures. Higher energy costs would not only raise the headline CPI but also erode disposable income, potentially dampening consumer spending and slowing the modest retail gains seen in recent months.

Financial markets have already begun to price in the uncertainty. The S&P 500 slipped 1.2 percent in early trading following the announcement of the strike, while Treasury yields rose as investors demanded a premium for perceived risk. The dollar, traditionally a safe‑haven currency, strengthened against the euro and yen, a move that could make imports cheaper but also hurt U.S. exporters. Moreover, the Federal Reserve may feel compelled to reassess its pause strategy if inflation re‑accelerates, which could lead to another round of rate hikes and further tighten credit conditions.

Looking ahead, the trajectory of the U.S. economy will hinge on how quickly diplomatic channels can de‑escalate the conflict and whether oil markets can stabilize. If the war remains limited and supply chains stay intact, the modest inflation decline could continue, allowing the Fed to maintain its current stance and giving households breathing room. Conversely, a protracted or broadened conflict could reignite price pressures, force a policy pivot, and stall the fragile consumer confidence that has been the engine of recent growth. Policymakers, investors and everyday Americans will be watching closely as the next few weeks determine whether the brief economic optimism of February becomes a lasting trend or a fleeting interlude before a new bout of volatility.
